summary: This episode discusses the Prophet's ﷺ childhood in the village of Banu Sa'd, especially play, and links it to today's crisis of children who do not play enough. Drawing on the books Chutzpah, The Anxious Generation and Hidden Potential, the ustaz explains that the first five years shape the brain, that free play, taking risks, resolving conflicts oneself and doing chores build confidence and emotional intelligence, and that slow growth is better than rushing. He then tells the hadith of Anas ibn Malik about the splitting of the Prophet's ﷺ chest while he played, Halimah's worry, and the Prophet being returned to Aminah. The ustaz closes with the Prophet's love for his mother, the fact that even the best childhoods meet loss, and a call for us to put our children's childhood first.
keyPoints: One of the biggest crises for children today is that they do not play enough, or are robbed of the chance and space to play.
Nearly 70 to 80 percent of the brain develops in the first two years and about 95 percent by age five, so the early phase is critical for brain wiring.
Open-ended play without direction, taking risks, resolving fights oneself and doing chores build confidence, creativity and emotional intelligence.
The Prophet ﷺ played all day in the village of Banu Sa'd with friends, and often expressed joy at playing with children.
The hadith of Anas ibn Malik tells how Jibril split the Prophet's ﷺ chest while he played, took out the share of Satan and washed the heart with Zamzam water.
Halimah returned the Prophet to Aminah out of fear, and Aminah reassured her with the story of the light that appeared when he was carried.
Long-term relationships with mentors, teachers and friends matter greatly, and children need attention during moves and separations.

chapters.summary: The brain develops rapidly until five, and The Anxious Generation recommends returning to a play-based childhood.

chapters.title: Open-ended play and toys
chapters.summary: Children in Israel play in junkyards without ready-made toys; toys that limit imagination do not help.

chapters.title: Taking risks and overprotection
chapters.summary: Teenage anxiety is linked to too few chances to take risks, and the ustaz shares his own experience of coming home from school.

chapters.title: Independence and resolving conflict
chapters.summary: Japanese children who shop on their own, and letting children settle their own fights.

chapters.title: Shaymaa and play in the Prophet's time
chapters.summary: The Prophet's foster sister was recognised after the Conquest of Mecca by a bite mark on her back.

chapters.title: Learning through play and emotional intelligence
chapters.summary: Children learn to respond, wait their turn and read body language through play.

chapters.title: Long-term relationships and mentors
chapters.summary: Long relationships with teachers and friends, the story of Musa and Khidr, and the Prophet ﷺ and Companions as mentorship.

chapters.title: Chores and adult success
chapters.summary: Long-term studies show children who do chores are more successful.

chapters.title: Halimah and the Prophet returned to the village
chapters.summary: Halimah begged to add two more years, and the Prophet's ﷺ eloquent Arabic from the village of Banu Sa'd.

chapters.title: Anas ibn Malik and the Prophet's ﷺ upbringing
chapters.summary: Anas served ten years and was never scolded by the Prophet; he joined children at play.

chapters.summary: Aminah reassured Halimah, and the ustaz closes with lessons on putting childhood first and loss in the Prophet's ﷺ life.

books.context: Studies how children are raised in Israel, the most innovative country. The ustaz was introduced to the book by his mentor and says children are left to play freely, take risks and fight.
Cited on the shift from a phone-based childhood to a play-based one, slow growth, and the risks linked to teenage anxiety.

books.context: Mentioned on long-term relationships with supervisors and mentors that build potential.

people.context: Studies how children are raised in Israel.

people.role: Foster sister of the Prophet ﷺ
people.context: Captured after the Conquest of Mecca and recognised by the Prophet through the bite mark on her back.
Studies the effect of mentors and long-term relationships on learning.
Mentions the Prophet's smile that was really anger after he stayed behind from the Battle of Tabuk.

people.role: Foster mother of the Prophet ﷺ
people.context: Raised the Prophet in the village of Banu Sa'd, begged to extend the period, then sent him home out of worry after the splitting of the chest.
Sent by his mother to the Prophet ﷺ at age ten and served him for ten years without ever being scolded.
Came while the Prophet ﷺ played and split his chest according to Anas's hadith.
Reassured Halimah by mentioning the light that came from her womb as far as Sham.

lessons.title: Give children room to play freely
lessons.body: Play is how children get to know the world; toys that direct too much limit imagination and creativity.

lessons.title: Don't rush early education
lessons.body: We tend to speed up children's writing and memorising before time, even though the Prophet ﷺ allowed children to play first.

lessons.title: Give room to take risks
lessons.body: Overprotection causes anxiety and loss of confidence; children need to learn independence, like shopping on their own.

lessons.title: Let children resolve conflicts themselves
lessons.body: Parents need not be referees; children learn to apologise and settle matters themselves.

lessons.title: Play builds emotional and social intelligence
lessons.body: Children learn to wait their turn, read body language and respond through direct interaction.

lessons.title: Long relationships build potential
lessons.body: Changing friends and schools too often prevents bonding; long mentorship is the best way to learn.

lessons.title: Chores build adult success
lessons.body: Long-term studies show children who do chores are more successful and stable in relationships.

lessons.title: Give attention when children move and part
lessons.body: Parting from friends and old places is very hard; give a year or two for a child to adapt.

lessons.title: Put children's childhood first, even if you must downgrade
lessons.body: Consider lowering your lifestyle for a more meaningful life for your children, without worrying too much about what people say.

lessons.title: Even the best childhood does not avoid loss
lessons.body: The Prophet ﷺ experienced the loss of his mother, yet a solid foundation prepared him for a great trust.

glossary.meaning: A childhood that develops slowly, not hurried, especially from birth to puberty.
A Hebrew word for boldness and resilience; the title of a book on how children are raised in Israel.
Open-ended play without rules or direction from adults.
Protecting a child so much that they are not given the chance to take risks and learn.
The skill of resolving fights, learned when children are left to settle them on their own.

dalil.context: The ustaz uses it to show that the Companions could read the Prophet's ﷺ face, as an example of emotional intelligence from long-term relationships.
dalil.translation: Ka'b ibn Malik, who stayed behind from the Battle of Tabuk, mentions that the Prophet ﷺ smiled at him, but the smile of someone angry.

dalil.context: The ustaz mentions it as an effect of playing and communicating with other children in that village.
dalil.translation: The Prophet ﷺ said he was the Arab with the best language because he was raised in the village of Banu Sa'd.

dalil.context: The ustaz says this hadith was narrated by Imam Muslim from Anas ibn Malik, and stresses that he was playing when it happened.
dalil.translation: Anas ibn Malik narrated that Jibril came to the Prophet ﷺ while he was playing with his friends, laid him down, split open his chest, took out the heart and a portion, and said this is the share of Satan from you, then washed it with Zamzam water in a golden basin and put it back. Anas said he saw the mark of the stitching on his chest.

dalil.context: The ustaz says the Prophet was prepared through his childhood before leading all the worlds as a mercy. The verse number is not mentioned. (reference identified; verse number not mentioned)
dalil.translation: It was only as a mercy that We sent you [Prophet] to all people.

dalil.context: The ustaz mentions it as evidence of deep affection and that loss was experienced by the Prophet himself.
dalil.translation: The Prophet ﷺ visited his mother's grave and wept uncontrollably until his beard was wet, and the Companions wept too.
